areas.n: Center City, Old City & the Parkway
South Philly (Italian Market, Passyunk, Washington Ave)
Northeast Philly (Port Richmond, Little Brazil, Cottman Ave)

cuisines.n: Bakeries, Soft Pretzels, Water Ice & Desserts

P.w: Where the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the Constitution (1787) were debated and signed — a UNESCO World Heritage Site run by the National Park Service; free timed tickets.
The 2,080-lb cracked bell, an abolitionist-adopted icon of liberty, displayed in an NPS pavilion facing Independence Hall; free.

P.ad: S 6th St & Chestnut St, Philadelphia, PA 19106
P.w: Where the US Congress met for ten years (1790–1800) while Philadelphia was the nation's capital; Washington's second and Adams' inauguration happened here. NPS-ranger tours.
The 1770s guild hall where the First Continental Congress met in 1774; free, still owned by the Carpenters' Company.
Franklin Court: Robert Venturi's steel 'ghost structures' outlining Franklin's lost house, the underground Benjamin Franklin Museum and a working 18th-century printing office.

P.ad: S 6th St & Market St, Philadelphia, PA 19106
P.w: Open-air memorial on the footprint of the house where Washington and Adams lived in the 1790s — and where Washington held nine enslaved Africans; exhibits on liberty and slavery. Free.

P.n: Second Bank of the United States Portrait Gallery
P.w: A Greek Revival marvel (1824) housing 150+ portraits of the founding era's politicians, explorers and society leaders, many by Charles Willson Peale.
Built 1727–44, the Anglican church where George Washington, Benjamin Franklin and Betsy Ross worshipped; its steeple was once the tallest structure in the colonies.
Benjamin Franklin's grave — visitors toss pennies on it for luck — among five signers of the Declaration buried here.
Continuously inhabited since 1720 — one of America's oldest residential streets: 32 craftsmen's houses, two of them a small museum.
The 1740s home of America's most famous upholsterer and flag-maker; tiny rooms, tight stairs and the story of the flag.
Steps from Independence Hall, it traces the colonies from unrest to independence; centrepiece is George Washington's original headquarters tent.
The world's only museum dedicated to the US Constitution, with Signers' Hall's 42 life-size bronze framers.

P.n: Philadelphia Museum of Art & the Rocky Steps
P.w: One of the largest art museums in the US (Renaissance to Duchamp) atop the 72 steps Rocky Balboa ran in 1976 — the Rocky statue stands at the bottom.
Albert Barnes' collection hung in his idiosyncratic 'ensembles': one of the world's greatest holdings of Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse beside African art and ironwork.
Opened 1829 as the world's first true 'penitentiary' (solitary reform), closed 1971, now a crumbling, haunting museum — Al Capone's cell is furnished.
Isaiah Zagar's labyrinthine folk-art environment of mirror, tile and bottle mosaics — half a block of it — on South Street.
America's great public market, under a former railroad trainshed since 1893: roast pork, Amish counters, Bassetts ice cream and 70-plus merchants.
One of the largest public Rodin collections outside Paris, fronted by bronze casts of The Thinker and The Gates of Hell; garden free.
Philadelphia's hands-on science museum — walk-through Giant Heart, Baldwin locomotive, planetarium — and home of the national Benjamin Franklin Memorial.

P.n: Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University
P.w: America's oldest natural-science research institution (1812): Dinosaur Hall and a live butterfly room.
The Free Library's Beaux-Arts flagship on Logan Square; its Rare Book Department and rooftop terrace are open to visitors.
Alexander Stirling Calder's 1924 fountain whose three Native American figures represent the Delaware, Schuylkill and Wissahickon — the centrepiece of Logan Circle.
The bronze Rocky Balboa from Rocky III, at the foot of the Art Museum steps — the city's most-photographed statue. Free.
The College of Physicians' museum of medical oddities — America's most famous — with slides of Einstein's brain, the Soap Lady and a wall of skulls.

P.n: Edgar Allan Poe National Historic Site
P.w: The only surviving Philadelphia home of Poe, with the cobwebbed cellar that may have inspired 'The Black Cat'; NPS-run, free.
A Victorian natural-history museum preserved intact since the 1890s — cherrywood cases, the first American saber-toothed-cat fossil found by Joseph Leidy; free.

P.ad: Lansdowne Dr & Horticultural Dr, Philadelphia, PA 19131
P.w: A 17th-century-style shoin house sent from Japan as a postwar gift of peace, with a tiered waterfall and koi pond; open late March–October, Wed–Sun.
Fifteen 19th-century rowing-club boathouses on the east bank of the Schuylkill, outlined in LED lights after dark — the city's postcard view from Kelly Drive.
America's first zoo (1874): ~1,900 animals on 42 Victorian-garden acres, with Zoo360 trails letting big cats and primates cross above visitors.

P.ad: 4231 Avenue of the Republic, Philadelphia, PA 19131
P.w: Children's museum inside Memorial Hall, the Beaux-Arts survivor of the 1876 Centennial Exposition, with a restored 1908 Dentzel carousel.

P.n: Mann Center for the Performing Arts
P.w: Open-air amphitheatre in West Fairmount Park, the Philadelphia Orchestra's summer home, with lawn seats facing the skyline.
One of America's oldest playgrounds, home of the c.1899 Ann Newman Giant Wooden Slide (60 ft long) — free.
Largest of Fairmount Park's historic houses, built 1789 by abolitionist judge William Lewis, Greek Revival wings c.1828, with an antique-doll collection.

The University of Pennsylvania's museum of archaeology and anthropology: 1M+ artifacts incl. Queen Puabi's gold-and-lapis headdress from Ur (c.2550 BC), a 12-ton Sphinx and the largest set of Maya stelae in the US.
North America's oldest surviving botanic garden, John Bartram's 18th-century riverside farm — 45+ acres on the Schuylkill with the continent's oldest living ginkgo; free.
Penn's free contemporary-art museum (1963), which gave Andy Warhol his first museum show and keeps championing emerging artists.
2,000 wooded acres of gorge along Wissahickon Creek inside the city: 50 miles of trails, Forbidden Drive, a covered bridge and the 1850 Valley Green Inn.
Penn's 92-acre teaching arboretum on the former Morris estate — Japanese, English and wildflower gardens, the Out on a Limb canopy walk and a seasonal garden railway.
The 1760s Chew family estate that British troops fortified during the 1777 Battle of Germantown — re-enacted every October at the Revolutionary Germantown Festival.
A Chestnut Hill estate bequeathed as a museum devoted to Philadelphia artists, from the founder's collection to temporary shows.
Site of British North America's first paper mill (1690) — a cluster of 17th–18th-century stone houses in the Wissahickon.

P.ad: 1400 N Outer Line Dr, King of Prussia, PA 19406
P.w: Site of the Continental Army's 1777–78 winter encampment: 3,500 acres with Washington's original headquarters, reconstructed huts, the National Memorial Arch and miles of trails.
Pierre S. du Pont's 1,000-acre showpiece: a grand conservatory, Italian water garden and illuminated fountain shows, 9,000+ plant species.

P.ad: 1 Hoffman's Mill Rd, Chadds Ford, PA 19317
P.w: A converted 19th-century grist mill on the Brandywine holding three generations of Wyeths (N.C., Andrew, Jamie), with tours of the N.C. Wyeth House & Studio.
Park on the field of the Revolution's largest land battle (Sept 11, 1777), with Washington's and Lafayette's quarters.
Henry Chapman Mercer's eccentric hand-poured-concrete castle (1908–12): 44 rooms, 32 staircases and 18 fireplaces, built without plans and lined with his own tiles.
Mercer's six-storey concrete castle of pre-industrial America — thousands of tools, vehicles and looms hung from a soaring central court.
Mercer's mission-style tile factory, still making his Moravian tiles by hand; the third stop on the 'Mercer Mile'.
Bucks County art — the New Hope Pennsylvania Impressionists above all — in the renovated 19th-century county jail.
Where Washington's army crossed the icy Delaware on Christmas night 1776 before Trenton; re-enacted every December 25.
William Penn's reconstructed country estate on the Delaware, with living-history farm and gardens.
Camden waterfront aquarium with hippos, penguins, sharks and the Shark Bridge — rated one of the best US aquariums by Travel Channel.
The Iowa-class USS New Jersey — built at the Philadelphia Navy Yard and launched in 1942, America's most decorated battleship — a museum ship since 2001.
The modest 1848 house where Walt Whitman lived from 1884 until his death in 1892, still holding his belongings; free tours.
Camden's riverfront promenade with the best straight-on view of the Philadelphia skyline across the Delaware.
Four-acre interactive garden for kids on the Camden waterfront, next to the aquarium.
1750 tavern where New Jersey's legislature met in 1777 and adopted the state seal — now a free state-run museum in downtown Haddonfield.

P.ad: S 9th St & Christian St, Philadelphia, PA 19147
P.w: America's oldest open-air street market: awning-covered blocks of family butchers, fishmongers, cheese shops and bakeries, now with Mexican, Vietnamese and Korean kitchens alongside.
Year-round home of the sequined New Year's Day Mummers Parade, on 'Two Street' near the clubhouses.
One of the oldest community art schools in the US (1898), with a Romanesque-revival sanctuary gallery open free.
The immigrant landing pier once called Philadelphia's Ellis Island, now a wetland boardwalk with Jody Pinto's 55-ft 'Land Buoy' lookout.

P.n: Barnes Arboretum at Saint Joseph's University
P.w: Laura Barnes' 12-acre arboretum at the Barnes Foundation's original Merion home — 2,500+ species, some planted in the 1880s.
A 35-acre 'pleasure garden' on a Main Line estate, named among America's top-10 public gardens; open Wed–Sun in season.
Raymond Pitcairn's medieval-style castle-home, one of the nation's largest museums of religious art (~8,000 works) — part of the Bryn Athyn National Historic Landmark district.
A Gothic-Romanesque cathedral built by medieval craft methods (1913–19), centrepiece of the Bryn Athyn Historic District.

P.ad: 824 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA 19010
P.w: A restored 1926 movie house turned nonprofit art cinema — one of the Main Line's signature institutions.

1,600 acres of creek valley woods and meadows in the Northeast — trails, horseback riding, birding at the Pennypack Environmental Center and the 1697 Frankford Avenue Bridge, the oldest stone road bridge in the US.
The city's last 19th-century riverfront estate open to the public: a Torresdale mansion and 18 acres of gardens where Poquessing Creek meets the Delaware.
A free Victorian villa museum in Burholme Park with the Ryerss family's eclectic collection of Asian art, paintings and heirlooms; open Fri–Sun.
One of the few working farms left inside a major US city — sheep shearing, Maple Sugar Day and Applefest.
Riverfront park on the spot where, by legend, William Penn made his 1683 treaty with the Lenape under an elm; skyline views and an obelisk.
Fishtown's big concert hall in a converted foundry, with the smaller Foundry upstairs — touring acts and dance parties.

P.ad: 1400 John F Kennedy Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19107
P.w: The largest municipal building in the US, crowned by Alexander Milne Calder's 37-ft William Penn; a 100-year-old elevator lifts four at a time to the glass-enclosed deck 548 ft up, the city's only 360° view.

P.ad: 1599 John F Kennedy Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19102
P.w: John F. Kennedy Plaza, nicknamed for Robert Indiana's LOVE sculpture — one of Philly's most photographed spots, diagonal from City Hall. Free.
One of William Penn's five original squares, named for astronomer David Rittenhouse — the elegant heart of Center City for benches, people-watching and the Saturday farmers' market.
Penn's southeast square, a Revolutionary-era burial ground now holding the Tomb of the Unknown Revolutionary War Soldier; part of Independence NHP.
The 1873 Norman-cathedral-style headquarters of Pennsylvania's Freemasons across from City Hall, with seven lavish lodge halls in Egyptian, Moorish, Gothic and other styles; public tours.
Neoclassical waterworks pavilions (1815–) on the Schuylkill below the Art Museum — a National Historic Landmark with a free interpretive center and the classic river-and-boathouse view.

P.n: Cathedral Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul
P.w: Pennsylvania's largest Catholic church (1864) and the only US cathedral in the Roman-Corinthian style, modelled on Rome's San Carlo al Corso, on Logan Square.
Rafael Viñoly's glass-vaulted arts centre (2001); its cello-shaped, mahogany Marian Anderson Hall is home to the Philadelphia Orchestra, and the rooftop garden is free.
America's oldest grand opera house still used for its original purpose (1857): gilded, chandeliered home of Opera Philadelphia and the Pennsylvania Ballet.

P.n: Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts (PAFA)
P.w: The nation's first art museum and school (1805), in Frank Furness's Victorian Gothic landmark fronted by Claes Oldenburg's 51-ft Paint Torch — American art from Peale to the present.
Mother church of the first Black denomination in the US (founded 1787 by Richard Allen) on the oldest parcel continuously owned by African Americans; the basement museum holds Allen's tomb.
Free-standing 1786 Federal mansion of Dr. Philip Syng Physick, 'father of American surgery', who treated Dolley Madison and Andrew Jackson — with the instruments he invented.
One of the finest Georgian townhouses in America (1765), where Mayor Samuel Powel and Elizabeth Willing Powel entertained Washington, Adams and Franklin.
The largest Quaker meeting house in the world by seating (1803–04), whose abolitionist congregation expelled members who would not free enslaved people.
A Quaker family's 1768 house that became a key Underground Railroad station (Harriet Tubman is said to have stopped here) — a National Historic Landmark.
Quaker homestead begun 1690 — Revolution-era field hospital, later a brewery — whose 1820s rose garden is the nation's oldest in its original plan.
The 1744 Wister family house, British General Agnew's quarters in 1777, with North America's oldest female ginkgo in the garden.
America's second-oldest rural garden cemetery (1836): 74 sculpted acres of Victorian monuments high above the Schuylkill in East Falls — tours and moonlight events.
Where George Washington lived in 1793–94 to escape the yellow-fever epidemic — the oldest surviving presidential residence; NPS-run.

P.ad: 8231 Old York Rd, Elkins Park, PA 19027
P.w: Frank Lloyd Wright's only synagogue (1954–59), a translucent glass-and-steel 'mountain of light' — one of four synagogues in the US that are National Historic Landmarks; tours by appointment.
650 acres of woods, meadows and old trees with 17 miles of trails — one of the region's oldest and largest public gardens, with giant treehouses for kids.
Pennsylvania's oldest church (1700), built by Swedish colonists in Queen Village — a National Historic Site with a riverside churchyard.

P.ad: 1 Lincoln Financial Field Way, Philadelphia, PA 19148
P.w: Home of the Eagles in the South Philadelphia Sports Complex — tailgate culture at its loudest.
The Phillies' ballpark, where the concourse food is a Philly tour in itself (cheesesteaks, roast pork, Bull's BBQ) and the Liberty Bell lights up for home runs.
Olmsted Brothers-designed lakes-and-lawns park at the bottom of Broad Street, with the Swedish-American Museum next door and a skatepark under I-95.
The nation's first naval shipyard turned office-and-park campus with a central green and Delaware riverfront; the USS New Jersey was built here.

P.ad: 301 S Christopher Columbus Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19106
P.w: Penn's Landing's summer pop-up park — hammocks, floating barge gardens, a beer garden, food stalls and glowing lights over the Delaware (seasonal).

P.ad: 211 S Christopher Columbus Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19106
P.w: Philadelphia's maritime museum at Penn's Landing; board the cruiser Olympia (Dewey's flagship at Manila Bay, 1898) and the WWII submarine Becuna.
The 1926 suspension bridge to Camden — then the world's longest suspension span — walkable on its south deck, lit at night; best seen from Race Street Pier.
Nine-acre West Philly commons: year-round farmers' market, Shakespeare in Clark Park and summer movies, with a Dickens statue.
William Hamilton's 18th-century Federal mansion and a 54-acre Victorian garden cemetery (Thomas Eakins is buried here) — a National Historic Landmark open dawn to dusk.
Penn's 1895 stadium — the oldest US stadium still used for football and home of the Penn Relays, the oldest US track meet.
An 18th-century Fairmount Park mansion now housing the Underground Railroad Museum, beside Belmont Plateau's famous skyline view.
Henry Francis du Pont's 175-room country house holding one of the world's great collections of American decorative arts, set in 1,000 acres of naturalistic garden and meadow.
The original 1802 DuPont black-powder works on the Brandywine — mills, the Georgian du Pont ancestral home and gardens on a ~2-hour tour.
Alfred I. du Pont's Louis XVI-style mansion with the largest French formal garden in North America, fountains and period rooms.

P.ad: 70 S Main St, New Hope, PA 18938
P.w: 'America's most famous summer theater', opened 1939 in a former grist mill on the Delaware in New Hope (Travel + Leisure's 2024 Best Small Arts Town); year-round productions.
A colonial-style village of 70+ shops, restaurants and pubs with Giggleberry Fair for kids and seasonal festivals, just outside New Hope.
Sesame Street theme park for young kids — rides, water play and shows; the first theme park designated a Certified Autism Center.
The Biddle family's Greek Revival mansion (early 19th c.) and 65 acres of formal gardens and woods on the Delaware.
The 1903 movie palace where the audience fled the theatre in 1958's The Blob — every July it hosts Blobfest and re-stages the run-out; arthouse films year-round on Phoenixville's Bridge Street.
The 'plain massive stone temple' Whitman designed for himself after Blake's 'Death's Door' — its door kept ajar so his soul is free — in 130-acre Harleigh Cemetery on the Cooper River.
Where one of the world's first nearly complete dinosaur skeletons was dug up in 1858 — a National Historic Landmark marker in a Haddonfield ravine (the town also has a Hadrosaurus statue downtown).

National Historic Landmark department-store palace whose Grand Court houses the Wanamaker Organ, the world's largest operating musical instrument (28,750 pipes); after Macy's closed in 2025 the new owners brought back performances and the Christmas Light Show (Inquirer, Philly Mag 2025).
The oldest operating theatre in the US (1808) and a National Historic Landmark — first gas footlights in 1837; still stages plays and Tony-winning musicals each season.
Rare-book house museum near Rittenhouse holding Joyce's handwritten Ulysses manuscript, Lewis Carroll's own Alice and a first-edition Don Quixote (Visit Philly; Philly Mag Best of Philly).
One of William Penn's five original squares, revived 20 years ago with a carousel, Philly-landmark mini golf and the winter Chinese Lantern Festival (Visit Philly; Inquirer 2026).
James Logan's c.1730 Georgian estate — both Washington and Howe headquartered here around the Battle of Germantown; on the Historic Germantown OnePass (Visit Philly; Billy Penn 2026).
Philadelphia's only Victorian house museum (1859), open Fri-Sun (Visit Philly Germantown guide; Hidden City).
Free 55-acre Quaker-abolitionist Cope family estate opened to the public in 1916 — 2,000+ trees, a working farm and gardens (Visit Philly; Hidden City).
1775 schoolhouse, Philadelphia's first English-language school and an 1839 abolitionist meeting place; tours second Saturdays May-Oct (Visit Philly Black-history guide).

P.ad: Thomas Mill Rd at Forbidden Drive, Wissahickon Valley Park, Philadelphia, PA 19118
P.w: The Wissahickon's red covered bridge on the Orange Trail, loved enough to get its own Inquirer column of love letters (Atlas Obscura; Inquirer; Philly Mag Wissahickon guide).

Revolutionary War fort at the mouth of the Schuylkill whose 1777 siege bought Washington time — barracks, blacksmith shop and weekend cannon demonstrations, open Wed-Sun March to mid-December (Visit Philly; Atlas Obscura unusual history).
Swedish-American culture museum tucked into FDR Park, near the site of the 1640s New Sweden colony (Visit Philly hidden gems).

National Historic Landmark and one of the finest Greek Revival buildings in America; its museum tells the story of Stephen Girard and the school's desegregation fight (open Wed-Fri; Visit Philly Black-history guide).

P.ad: Frankford Ave over Pennypack Creek, Holmesburg, Philadelphia, PA 19136
P.w: Built in 1697 — the oldest surviving roadway bridge in the US and probably the country's oldest stone arch bridge, still carrying Frankford Ave traffic (Atlas Obscura; Inquirer).
75+ of the world's rarest racing sports cars collected by Dr. Fred Simeone over 50 years — a one-of-a-kind museum by the airport (Visit Philly hidden gems).

P.n: John Heinz National Wildlife Refuge at Tinicum
P.w: Pennsylvania's largest freshwater tidal marsh, 10+ miles of trails and Darby Creek paddling inside the city limits (Visit Philly hidden gems).

The 1934 Neoclassical rail palace — limestone façade, prism-glass windows and the bronze Angel of the Resurrection WWII memorial; on Architectural Digest's most-beautiful-stations list (Visit Philly architecture guide).

P.n: Fisher Fine Arts Library & Arthur Ross Gallery
P.w: Frank Furness's red sandstone and terra-cotta Venetian Gothic library on Penn's campus, home to the Arthur Ross Gallery (Visit Philly University City guide).

Once Pennsylvania's largest burial ground (85,000 graves, 200 acres, Betsy Ross's former resting place), now being reclaimed from the woods by the volunteer Friends of Mount Moriah (Visit Philly strange & unusual guide).
Horace Trumbauer's Art Deco theatre in Glenside, still booking major music, theatre and comedy acts (Visit Philly Jenkintown guide).
1722 manor of Pennsylvania governor William Keith, later seized from loyalist Henry Fergussen and poet Elizabeth Graeme; house and gardens open year-round (Valley Forge Tourism).

P.ad: 553 S Bethlehem Pike, Fort Washington, PA 19034
P.w: Early-Georgian mansion (1743-48) built by Quaker Samuel Morris — HQ of Washington's Surgeon General during the Whitemarsh Encampment (Valley Forge Tourism).
1704 home of Charles Thomson, Secretary of the Continental Congress and designer of the Great Seal, set in a park with gardens (Valley Forge Tourism).
Reconstruction of the boarding house at 7th & Market where Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1776 — part of Independence National Historical Park (NPS).
Dolley Madison's home with her first husband John Todd Jr. before his 1793 death — a restored middle-class Quaker house in Independence NHP (NPS).
The 1787 townhouse of Bishop William White, first Episcopal bishop of Pennsylvania — an upper-class counterpart to the Todd House in Independence NHP (NPS).
The smallest unit of the National Park System — the Society Hill boarding house where Polish patriot and Revolutionary War engineer Thaddeus Kościuszko lived in 1797-98 (NPS).
Federal-style 1790-91 building in the Independence Hall complex that housed the US Supreme Court from 1791 to 1800 (NPS Independence NHP).
NPS-preserved 18th-19th-century iron-making village in the hills by French Creek State Park — furnace, ironmaster's house and orchards (National Park Service).

P.ad: 32 W Bridge St, New Hope, PA 18938
P.w: Heritage line between New Hope and Lahaska with antique coaches pulled by a 1925 Baldwin steam locomotive from the Witch's Hat Station (Visit Bucks County).
134 acres with nearly 1,000 native plant species, meadow, pond and a nationally recognised native-plant nursery; reservations required (Visit Bucks County).

P.n: Pearl S. Buck House (Green Hills Farm)
P.w: National Historic Landmark homestead of Nobel laureate Pearl S. Buck, with guided house tours (Visit Bucks County).

P.ad: Hermit Ln trail, Wissahickon Valley Park, Philadelphia, PA 19128
P.w: Stone-fronted hillside cave of the 1694 'Hermits of the Wissahickon' doomsday mystics led by Johannes Kelpius, on the trails at the park's south end (Atlas Obscura; Visit Philly strange & unusual; Hidden City).
Canal-edged former mill-town main street with ~275 shops, galleries, bars and restaurants, next to the Manayunk Canal towpath and the Schuylkill (Visit Philly; Inquirer Manayunk guide).

P.ad: Lemon Hill Dr & Poplar Dr, East Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, PA 19130
P.w: Neoclassical Fairmount Park villa with oval rooms and curved doors on all three floors — one of the four park houses open for tours (Hidden City; Philadelphia Museum of Art park-house guides).

P.ad: Ford Rd & Greenland Dr, East Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, PA 19121
P.w: c.1756 Georgian mansion of merchant William Coleman, Franklin's confidant, with one of the city's finest carved overmantels; open for tours (Visit Philly).

P.ad: Edgeley Dr, East Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, PA 19121
P.w: c.1767 Georgian 'Randolph House' high above the Schuylkill — the most visible of the park houses and one of four open for tours (Hidden City).

P.n: National Shrine of St. John Neumann
P.w: Lower church of St. Peter the Apostle holding the glass tomb of St. John Neumann, fourth bishop of Philadelphia and the first American man canonized — founder of the US diocesan school system (Visit Philly sacred-sites trail).
The nation's largest ceramic-arts organisation (founded ~50 years ago), now in a purpose-built Kensington home with exhibitions and classes (Visit Philly off-the-beaten-path museums; Inquirer).

130-year-old Victorian high-rise at Broad & Fairmount, one of the country's first racially integrated hotels, reopened after a $44M restoration with residences and a restaurant (Visit Philly North Broad guide).

P.n: Fairmount Park Horticulture Center & Centennial Arboretum
P.ad: 100 N Horticultural Dr, West Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, PA 19131
P.w: Greenhouse and arboretum on the site of the 1876 Centennial Exposition's Horticultural Hall, beside Shofuso (Visit Philly North Philly guide).

Oscar Hammerstein I's 1908 opera house, restored as a year-round concert and comedy venue (Live Nation since 2018) — neoclassical façade, chandeliers and tiered seating (Visit Philly North Broad guide).
El Centro de Oro's 50-year-old Puerto Rican arts and culture centre — gallery, performance and education space (Visit Philly North Philly / Latino sites guides).

Opened for the 1976 Bicentennial as the first museum built by a major US city to preserve African American heritage; permanent exhibit 'Audacious Freedom: African Americans in Philadelphia 1776-1876' (Visit Philly).

P.n: Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History
P.ad: 101 S Independence Mall E, Philadelphia, PA 19106
P.w: The only US museum dedicated exclusively to the American Jewish experience, on Independence Mall; renovating in 2026 with 'The First Salute' (Jewish connections to the Revolution) on view through April 2027 (Visit Philly).
Old City museum on American diversity and liberty, centred on Dale Chihuly's 21-ft glass 'Flame of Liberty' (Visit Philly).

P.ad: 2000 Valley Forge Park Rd, Valley Forge, PA 19481
P.w: Ornate chapel begun in 1903 inside Valley Forge park as a tribute to Washington and the encampment's soldiers — free entry to its stained glass and the suffrage-campaign Justice Bell; still an active parish (Valley Forge Tourism; Main Line Today).

P.n: John James Audubon Center at Mill Grove
P.w: Audubon's 18th-century American home with a 2019 museum of art and conservation; free grounds with 175+ bird species, trails and Saturday bird walks (Valley Forge Tourism).
Working 1704 grist mill in a 160-acre park with 8+ miles of woodland and meadow trails (Main Line Today parks & hiking guides).

Used and rare bookshop since 1946 — 300,000+ items on five floors of a two-century-old stone barn, named by Architectural Digest among the world's most beloved independent bookstores (Visit Philly hidden gems).
340 wooded acres in Roxborough with 3+ miles of trails, nature exhibits, an environmental-art gallery and a wildlife rehabilitation clinic (Visit Philly Northwest guide).

P.n: Pomona Hall & Camden County Historical Society
P.w: The Cooper family's 18th-century home plus the Camden County History Museum and African American History Room; Pomona Hall tours by reservation (Visit NJ; Inquirer).
44-acre Delaware River site of the 1777 American victory at Fort Mercer, with the fort's earthworks and the 1748 Whitall House field hospital (Visit NJ; Inquirer on its archaeology).

P.ad: N Park Dr, Pennsauken / Cherry Hill, NJ 08109
P.w: 346-acre park around an Olympic-distance rowing course — bike loops, boathouse, mini golf and picnic grounds; a NJ 'Great Public Space' (Visit NJ; Inquirer; NJ Monthly scenic walks).
Restored Federal-style Quaker farmhouse on 32 acres with outbuildings, herb garden and nature trails; tours April-November (Visit NJ; SJ Magazine historic homes).

Puerto Rican community garden in Norris Square born from a 1992 anti-drug cleanup, with la casita de las abuelas — a rural Puerto Rican house filled with objects from the island. Documented by the Smithsonian's Community of Gardens, WHYY and 6abc.

142-ft brick shot tower completed on July 4, 1808 — one of the first in the US, dripping molten lead into musket balls for the War of 1812; now ringed by the city's Shot Tower Playground in Queen Village.

F.w: The South Philly shack (open since the 1930s) that Craig LaBan named the city's best cheesesteak in 2002 and that finished second in the Inquirer's 2023 bracket; its juicy roast pork with sautéed spinach earned a James Beard America's Classics award.

F.ad: Reading Terminal Market, 51 N 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19107
F.w: Reading Terminal Market's roast-pork counter — #1 on Philadelphia Magazine's roast-pork list and The Infatuation's pick for the best sandwich in the market.
Italian Market sandwich counter serving roast pork on Sarcone's rolls with a choice of American, mild or sharp provolone, or Whiz — on both Visit Philly's and Philly Mag's roast-pork lists.
Century-old 9th Street bakery whose tomato pie, baked in a brick hearth oven, is crisp at the edges and juicy in the middle; its seeded rolls carry half the city's hoagies and roast pork.

Tomato pie pulled from a 115-year-old, 21-foot-deep brick oven, topped with a classic South Philly red gravy balanced with garlic, oregano and Pecorino Romano. Note: open only on a few announced days a year — check before going.
On the corner of 7th and Christian since 1945, making water ice from nothing but water, sugar and fresh fruit.
Started in 1995 by a Temple student; a West Philly favourite for water ice loaded with chunks of real fruit.

F.ad: Reading Terminal Market, 51 N 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19107
F.w: America's oldest ice-cream company (1861), run by the fifth and sixth generations of L.D. Bassett's family — it predates the market itself.

F.ad: Reading Terminal Market, 51 N 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19107
F.w: Pennsylvania Dutch doughnuts since 1985 — around 40 varieties a day, stuffed, topped and drizzled, worth the line.

F.ad: Reading Terminal Market, 51 N 12th St, Philadelphia, PA 19107
F.w: Amish-family Pennsylvania Dutch counter where you sit elbow-to-elbow; get the plate-sized blueberry pancakes.
